USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the existing $50B in 25% tariffs as leverage but do not trigger the full $200B/25% List 3 escalation. Re-engage the Chinese trade delegation and push for a negotiated package (larger US purchases, verifiable IP/tech-transfer commitments) from a position of strength, while protecting the farm belt ahead of the midterms with the $12B aid program already in place.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate, not existential. US macro data remain robust at the decision date — industrial production is rising (104.1 in Sept), consumer sentiment is high at 100.1, and the broad dollar index is strong at 114.7 with the 2s10s still positive — so there is no recession signal from the trade war yet. What drives the threat reading is the concentrated damage to agriculture: China's 25% tariff on US soybeans (the largest US export to China, ~$12.4B/yr, ~60% of US ag exports to China) has pushed soybean prices down ~22% since April, farm income to a 12-year low, and generated acute political pressure in red-state farm districts ahead of the November midterms (the American Soybean Association and farmers themselves are lobbying Washington to halt escalation). Escalating to the full $200B at 25% would invite China's threatened $60B retaliation, which Beijing has explicitly aimed at US coffee, honey and industrial chemicals — hitting more farming/mining regions that voted for the administration. That overrides the temptation to press the escalation. However, the US holds clear leverage that justifies negotiating rather than conceding: China is running low on retaliation room (only ~$120B of US goods available for countermeasures, hence the smaller $60B threat) and will need US soybeans in Q4 once the Brazilian crop is exhausted, and the dollar's strength and strong domestic demand give us bargaining position. The stance is therefore to negotiate from strength — keep the $50B, avoid the self-defeating $200B/25% trigger, and extract concessions — which is why the action score sits near neutral-positive (hold/negotiate) rather than escalation.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Prepare a calibrated, proportionate retaliation for the imminent ~$200B List 3 tariff round — matching the two ~$50B rounds already in force and delivering on our stated ~$60B counter-threat — while simultaneously keeping a negotiation channel open so the spiral does not deepen further than Washington's own initiated action. We must defend credibility and deterrence (we have retaliated dollar-for-dollar at every step), but we should not chase maximal escalation we cannot win, since our export base to the US is far larger than US exports to us.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high but not existential. The US has already imposed 25% tariffs on ~$50B of our goods (List 1, ~$34B, effective 2018-07-06; List 2, ~$16B, effective 2018-08-23), which we matched in kind both times — evidence that the dispute is actively biting, not just rhetorical. Directly ahead, the US$200B List 3 public-comment period closes 2018-09-06 and tariffs could take effect 'as soon as Friday,' with the rate possibly rising from 10% to 25%, and Trump has threatened over $500B in total. This is a major escalation target at our core electronics/components, machinery, autos and consumer-goods export sectors, and the April ZTE denial order shows firm-level/tech targeting (entity-list risk) is live. Macro confirms stress: the yuan has already depreciated ~7% since March on trade tensions, pressure PBOC reserves and raising financial-stability concerns (analysts warn a weaponized devaluation would backfire capital-flight/2015-style), even as exports to the US still account for roughly a fifth of our overseas shipments. This drives a threat reading of ~+0.55 (high: major export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level targeting). For action, escalation is asymmetric and costly — US exports to China are far smaller than our $506B in US-bound sales, so we cannot fully mirror a $200B round (we have only threatened $60B) — which means restraint-with-deterrence, not maximal escalation, is the correct stance: retaliate proportionately to preserve leverage and signal resolve, but avoid triggering a steeper $500B-plus cascade that would hurt our own economy and financial system more than it hurts Washington.
